author: homer
title: Odyssey
summary: Twenty-four books on the homecoming of Odysseus in the tenth year after the fall of Troy: his son's search for news of him, his release from Calypso and his stay among the Phaeacians, the tale of his wanderings, and his return to Ithaca and his revenge on the suitors.

1.title: Athena Visits Telemachus
1.greek: Θεῶν ἀγορά, Ἀθηνᾶς παραίνεσις πρὸς Τηλέμαχον, Μνηστήρων εὐωχία
1.summary: The poet calls on the Muse to tell of Odysseus. In the tenth year after Troy he is held by Calypso, and while Poseidon is away among the Ethiopians the gods resolve to bring him home. Athena goes to Ithaca in the likeness of Mentes, finds the suitors feasting in Odysseus' house, and urges Telemachus to call an assembly and sail to Pylos and Sparta for news of his father. Penelope asks Phemius to stop his song of the Achaeans' homecoming; Telemachus rebukes her and the suitors, and lies awake all night pondering his journey.

2.title: The Assembly of the Ithacans
2.summary: At dawn Telemachus calls the first assembly in Ithaca since Odysseus sailed and accuses the suitors before the people. Antinous blames Penelope and her trick of the web; Zeus sends two eagles, which the seer Halitherses reads as a sign that Odysseus is near, and Mentor rebukes the silent Ithacans, but the suitors refuse to leave. Athena, in the likeness of Mentor, promises Telemachus a ship and a crew; Eurycleia fills jars and bags for the voyage, and at nightfall he sails for Pylos with the goddess beside him.

3.title: At Pylos
3.summary: Telemachus and Athena, in the likeness of Mentor, reach Pylos as the Pylians sacrifice black bulls to Poseidon on the shore, and Nestor's son Peisistratus welcomes them. Nestor knows nothing of Odysseus, but he tells of the quarrel of the sons of Atreus and the homecomings of the Achaeans, of how Aegisthus won Clytemnestra and killed Agamemnon while Menelaus wandered as far as Egypt, and of Orestes' vengeance, and he urges Telemachus to go on to Menelaus. Athena leaves in the likeness of a sea eagle, and Nestor knows the goddess. The next morning he sacrifices to her a heifer with gilded horns, his daughter Polycaste bathes Telemachus, and Telemachus and Peisistratus drive by way of Pherae toward Sparta.

4.title: At Lacedaemon
4.summary: Telemachus and Peisistratus reach Sparta during a double wedding and are welcomed by Menelaus, who has gathered his wealth in eight years of wandering while his brother was murdered. Helen recognizes Odysseus' son, puts an Egyptian drug against grief into the wine, and tells how Odysseus entered Troy disguised as a beggar; Menelaus tells how Odysseus held the chieftains silent in the Wooden Horse. The next day Menelaus tells how, becalmed off Egypt, he seized Proteus, the Old Man of the Sea, and learned of the deaths of Ajax and Agamemnon, of Odysseus held by Calypso, and of his own destiny in the Elysian plain. In Ithaca the suitors discover the voyage and send a ship to ambush Telemachus on his way home; Penelope prays to Athena, and the goddess comforts her in a dream with a phantom of her sister Iphthime.

5.title: The Raft of Odysseus
5.summary: At a second council of the gods Athena pleads again for Odysseus, and Zeus sends Hermes to Calypso's island with the command that he be let go. Calypso protests at the jealousy of the gods but yields, and swears by the water of Styx that she plans him no harm; Odysseus refuses her offer of immortality and chooses his mortal wife and his home. In four days he builds a raft, and on the fifth he sails, steering by the stars. On the eighteenth day, within sight of the Phaeacians' land, Poseidon wrecks him with a storm; Ino, now the sea goddess Leucothea, gives him her immortal veil, and after two nights and two days in the sea he struggles ashore at the mouth of a river, prays to its god, and falls asleep under a heap of leaves between two olive bushes.

6.title: Odysseus Comes to the Phaeacians
6.summary: Athena comes in a dream to Nausicaa, daughter of Alcinous, king of the Phaeacians, and bids her wash her clothes against her marriage. At the river, after the washing and a game of ball, the girls' cry wakes Odysseus, who comes out of the bushes naked and caked with brine; the handmaids flee, but Nausicaa stands her ground. He begs her for help, likening her to Artemis and to the young palm on Delos, and she has him bathed, clothed and fed, while Athena makes him taller and more handsome. Nausicaa tells him the way to her father's house and bids him follow at a distance, for fear of gossip, and clasp her mother's knees; at sunset he waits in the grove of Athena and prays to her.

7.title: Odysseus at the House of Alcinous
7.summary: Athena, as a young girl, leads Odysseus through the city in a mist to the house of Alcinous and tells him to win the favor of Queen Arete. He marvels at the bronze house and the gardens that bear all year, clasps the queen's knees and sits in the ashes until Alcinous raises him, feasts him and promises an escort home. Arete knows the clothes he wears, and he tells of Calypso, the storm and his meeting with Nausicaa; Alcinous offers him his daughter and the swift Phaeacian ships.

8.title: Odysseus and the Phaeacians
8.summary: Alcinous orders a ship for the stranger's escort and a feast, where the blind singer Demodocus sings of the quarrel of Odysseus and Achilles and Odysseus hides his tears. At the games Euryalus taunts him, and he throws the discus beyond every mark. Demodocus sings of Ares and Aphrodite caught in Hephaestus' net; the Phaeacians give him gifts, and Nausicaa bids him farewell. When the singer, at his request, sings of the wooden horse, Odysseus weeps again, and Alcinous asks him who he is.

9.title: The Cyclops
9.summary: Odysseus names himself to the Phaeacians and begins the tale of his wanderings: the sack of Ismarus and the losses to the Cicones, the storm off Malea, the Lotus-eaters, and the land of the Cyclopes. Shut in the cave of Polyphemus, who eats six of his men, he makes him drunk with the wine of Maron, tells him that his name is Nobody, blinds him with a stake of olive wood, and escapes with his men under the rams. As they sail away he taunts the Cyclops and names himself, and Polyphemus prays to his father Poseidon that he may come home late and alone, to find bane in his house.

10.title: Aeolus, the Laestrygonians and Circe
10.greek: Τὰ περὶ Αἰόλου καὶ Λαιστρυγόνων καὶ Κίρκης
10.summary: Odysseus' tale goes on. Aeolus, keeper of the winds, gives him the winds shut in an oxhide skin and a fair breeze, but in sight of Ithaca his companions open the skin while he sleeps, and the storm drives them back; Aeolus sends him away as a man hated by the gods. The Laestrygonians destroy every ship but his own. On Aeaea the goddess Circe turns half his men into swine; with the moly that Hermes gives him Odysseus withstands her drugs, makes her swear an oath and restores them, and they stay a year. Circe tells him he must first go to the house of Hades to consult Teiresias; as they leave, the young Elpenor falls from her roof and dies.

11.title: The Land of the Dead
11.summary: Odysseus' tale goes on. At the edge of the world, by the stream of Oceanus, he digs a pit and pours the offerings to the dead, and the souls come up out of Erebus to drink the blood. He speaks with his unburied companion Elpenor, with the seer Teiresias, who foretells his homecoming and his last journey, and with his mother Anticleia, who died of longing for him; he sees the famous women of old. The tale breaks off in the hall of Alcinous, where Arete and Alcinous press him to stay and go on. He tells of the souls of Agamemnon, murdered by Aegisthus and his wife, of Achilles, who would rather be a hired man on earth than king of the dead, and of Ajax, who will not speak to him; of Minos, Orion, Tityus, Tantalus, Sisyphus and the phantom of Heracles; until fear drives him back to the ship.

12.title: The Sirens, Scylla and Charybdis, and the Cattle of the Sun
12.summary: The end of Odysseus' tale. Back on Aeaea he buries Elpenor, and Circe tells him the way home: past the Sirens, between Scylla and Charybdis, and to Thrinacia, where the cattle of the Sun must not be harmed. Bound to the mast he hears the Sirens' song; Scylla takes six of his companions; on Thrinacia, held by contrary winds and starving, the companions kill the Sun's cattle while he sleeps, and Zeus destroys the ship with his thunderbolt. Odysseus alone escapes Charybdis a second time and drifts to Calypso's island.
